title: Rowan and the Pickle-Scented Willow
markdown:
The towering peaks of the Whisperwind Range bit the air with frost, and when the sun chose to grace the sky it painted the snow in hues no earthly artist quite captured. Among crags that seemed to tickle the bellies of passing clouds lived Rowan. She was a witch, indeed, but not the cackling sort who brewed mischief for sport. Her magic was as practical as a well-mended cloak, as sensible as good sturdy boots. The cottage, tucked into the mountainside, smelled of dried herbs and baking bread and always sighed with hearth-warmth. By her side, always, was Mizzle.

Mizzle was a hedgehog, and not merely a hedgehog: Rowan’s familiar, quiet fortitude, remarkably sharp quills used for more than defence. He possessed a certain hedgehoggy wisdom. He understood subtle shifts of wind, the best forage routes, and, most importantly, Rowan — when a twinkle meant a good day brewing, and when it meant a mild magical mishap on the horizon. His tiny nose, a twitching compass of discernment, often nudged him toward her unspoken thoughts before she had finished having them.

This particular morning the air was crisp, promising a clear sky for a most important errand. Rowan needed a specific moonpetal for a restorative draught, a potent brew for Mrs. Gable down in the village, who had been suffering a particularly stubborn case of the sniffles. The finest moonpetals, shimmering with captured dew even on the driest days, grew only in the Sunken Glade, a mere half-day’s trek west, nestled in a hollow where the mountain’s shadow lay longest. “A simple matter, Mizzle,” she declared, fingers packing a sturdy wicker basket with a flask of fragrant chamomile, a small polished obsidian stone for luck — gift of a grateful gnome — and a neatly folded list of ingredients she might need to barter for. “Back before the shadows grow long, and Mrs. Gable sipping sunshine by supper.”

Mizzle huffed, dust from a forgotten book. His nose said life was rarely so straight, especially with certain enthusiastic apprentices.

The straight path developed a detour named Finn.

He bounced in like a runaway meteor, nearly rearranging Mizzle’s grey-pebble collection. “Master Rowan! Minor levitation, perfected! Observe!” Before caution could dress, he pointed at the basket. “Up!” A whoosh like a startled goose, off-key sparks smelling of burnt sugar: the basket shot up, snagged a beam carved with woodland spirits, and emptied ceramic and glass across the floor. Obsidian, flask, and the Sunken Glade list scattered among the pebbles.

“Enthusiastic,” Rowan sighed. Shoulders dipped a fraction. An escaped peppermint leaf jigged the boards.

“It worked!” Finn beamed, missing the quiet in her voice. “I’ll improve it!” The spilled tea tried to re-enter as a fountain and misted the ceiling floral.

“No.” She snatched the list from a fragrant puddle. “Sunken Glade. Moonpetals. Mrs. Gable.”

His eyes lit. “A quest! I’ll enhance. And lichen for practice.”

She pinched her nose, a gesture as familiar as her own brews. “Scenic route, then.” Mizzle was already nosing seeds into a pile, quills efficient.

Thus began the surprisingly complicated errand of the most practical of practitioners and her well-meaning, chaos-generating apprentice.

The path to the Sunken Glade, already made more circuitous by the basket’s unscheduled flight, led them along a winding goat track that hugged Mount Cinder — a giant of grey stone that seemed to scowl at the sky, peak often lost in a swirling cloak of mist. The air grew thinner with every step. The wind, a playful persistent prankster, tugged Rowan’s scarf and whispered through sparse pines. Chill seeped despite her enchanted weaving.

“Quite brisk. A minor warming charm. Gentle ambient heat.”

“I can!” Finn envisioned a personal sunbeam and produced a local heatwave. Moss steamed. Mizzle squeaked, unladylike, and burrowed into Rowan’s boot, spines out. The air went muggy.

“Less conflagration. Comfort.” She whispered a proper heat, a hug. Mizzle emerged, relieved, and grumbled thanks she heard without ears.

A sharp bend opened the world. The High Pass Market clung to the sheer face like wildflowers or a flamboyant flock of startled sheep: crimson, gold, sapphire banners on thin air; stalls of shimmer-cloth, humming instruments, jewel-fruit in precarious pyramids; spice, roast nut, something fizzy.

“I haven’t seen a bustle like this since Eldoria’s solstice.”

“Best deals!” Finn darted at enchanted trinkets. “Singing stones need resonance.”

“Do not improve the wares before we look.”

They descended into the bustling throng, a river of colourful cloaks and curious hats. Rowan needed a specific smooth-grained willow for the draught, weathered by mountain winds, carrying quiet strength — a task that required precision, not pizzazz. Mizzle, discreet observer, scurried at her heels, keen nose finding discarded cheese and dropped berries, a steady anchor in the swirl. The air buzzed with exotic spice, roasting nuts, and something vaguely fizzy. A stall of shimmering fabrics seemed to capture the thin light and refuse to give it back.

Finn, meanwhile, was in his element, a whirlwind of well-meaning disruption. He approached a vendor of small intricate wind chimes, each delicately crafted from polished bone and shimmering mica. “These are nice,” he declared, with the authority of one who knows exactly what is missing. “But imagine if they also sang sea shanties! The spirit of the ocean!” A flourish, a muttered incantation. The chimes, instead of rousing nautical tales, emitted a series of indignant squawks, startling a flock of mountain goats who had been enjoying a leisurely graze on the market’s refuse. The goats, quite understandably, scattered in a flurry of hooves and bleats that nearly took a pyramid of jewel-fruit with them.

“Focus. Willow. Smooth. Not shanties.”

The vendor, smile sharp, eyes amused, asked about singing chimes and a price. Rowan set a moon-kissed silver piece on the counter. “Passing through. If you have a sturdy branch, wind-smoothed, I might buy.”

A gap-tooth grin. She led them to a quiet corner. “Lightning last spring. Mostly harmless. Character.”

The grain was right; a faint hum. Finn, helpful: “Needs flair. Glow!” Emerald aura, vibration, a POP — the branch left the vendor and lodged in a barrel of pickled mountain onions. The barrel tipped. Onions and brine made a vinegary weather. Yelps, scurrying, near-misses.

Mizzle, pretzel-crumb interrupted, rode the onion tide and surfaced with a perfectly formed pickle on his nose, a very small, very grumpy king.

Rowan extracted the now onion-scented willow, paid a vendor wiping laugh-tears, and called it memorable. Finn offered a mending charm; onions reassembled lumpy; one plump specimen chose a merchant’s hat. She steered them from the disarray. “Fallen leaves for the rest of the practice. Stubborn cobwebs.”

With the onion-scented willow secured, and Finn already planning an improvement for the now onion-decorated barrel, Rowan steered them firmly away from the market’s delightful disarray. “Come along. We still have to reach the village. For the rest of the journey, practice on fallen leaves. Or particularly stubborn cobwebs.”

They continued the winding mountain path, the vibrant chaos a colourful blur below. Rowan’s errand had indeed become a scenic detour. The moonpetal seeds, scattered and then partly recovered, were not yet at the Sunken Glade. But the willow branch was found, albeit with a distinct vinegary aroma, and Mizzle, despite his onion-bathed ordeal, trotted beside her, the small onion still precariously balanced until a determined shake unseated it. And Finn — well, Finn was learning, in his own rather explosive and sometimes pungent way, and then, slowly, he stopped planning to improve the barrel.

They finally arrived at Oakhaven, nestled in a sheltered valley where chimneys puffed contented smoke-signals, tiny friendly clouds. The air here was thick with roast lamb and fresh bread, a welcome change from pickled onion. A festival occupied the square in full swing. Children chased with gleeful abandon, laughter like tiny joyous bells. Villagers shared stories and music, faces creased with smiles. Warm glow from every window promised comfort.

Rowan exchanged a look with Mizzle, who had finally dislodged the onion with a determined shake. “A celebration. What a weary witch and a faithful hedgehog need after unexpected scenery.”

Finn, finally subdued by the sheer abundance of food, accepted a generous honey cake from a kindly baker. “Better than singing wind chimes,” he admitted, mouth full, crumbs on his chin. Enhancements, for the moment, forgotten.

She sat a rustic bench. Mizzle groomed onion-scented quills with utmost seriousness. She watched the easy camaraderie, the simple noise of people not levitating baskets. The restorative draught, and Mrs. Gable’s sniffles, would wait until morning. The Glade would still be west, moonpetals still unfurling for whoever arrived with a list that had survived tea. For now there was cake, a hedgehog against her boot, an apprentice chewing instead of glowing things. The willow on her knee smelled of vinegar and lightning. She did not close the day with a promise about wisdom, or about tomorrow’s petals. She asked the baker for a second slice to travel, wrapped, and whether anyone had seen a barrel of onions that needed a lid. Finn, to his credit, went to help look, and did not offer to improve the lid first.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
